movement_note: Movement compares 2025 with 2024 GDP ranks for the same economies (inaugural edition). Revisions to past data are not counted as movement in this edition.

findings.title: The world economy reached US$118.35 trillion
findings.body: World GDP in 2025 came to US$118.35 trillion in current U.S. dollars. Measured across the economies with data for both years, dollar GDP rose 6.0% on 2024. (World total is the World Bank's world aggregate.)

findings.title: The U.S. alone is 26.00% of world output
findings.body: At US$30.77 trillion, the United States produced 26.00% of world GDP. Add China and the two account for 42.47%. The U.S. economy is 1.58 times the size of China's.

findings.title: The UK retook fifth place from India, narrowly
findings.body: The UK's US$4.00 trillion edged out India's US$3.96 trillion, even though India's real growth (+7.6%) outpaced the UK's (+1.4%). Both the World Bank and IMF figures put the UK ahead for 2025.

findings.title: India passes Japan and the UK in 2027, the IMF projects
findings.body: In the IMF's October 2026 forecasts, India reaches US$4.52 trillion in 2027, ahead of the UK (US$4.49 trillion) and Japan (US$4.47 trillion), making it the 4th-largest economy that year. In 2025, Japan was 4th and India 6th.

findings.title: The trillion-dollar club grew to 21
findings.body: 21 economies topped US$1 trillion in 2025, up from 19 in 2024. The newcomers: Switzerland (US$1.04 trillion) and Poland (US$1.04 trillion).

findings.title: Currency, not output, drove the biggest climb
findings.body: Ghana rose 10 places to 71st, the biggest climb in this edition. Its dollar GDP jumped 37.1% while real output grew +6.0%: most of the gain came from exchange-rate and price effects.

findings.title: Fast growth, falling rank
findings.body: Ethiopia's real economy grew +9.8%, the 6th-fastest rate in the world, yet it fell 7 places to 68th as its GDP measured in dollars dropped 15.6%.

findings.title: Ten economies hold 66.3% of world output
findings.body: The top 10 produced 66.3% of world GDP. The smallest 100 economies together produced 1.42%.

findings.title: China's economy is 15.9 times its 2000 size
findings.body: China grew from US$1.22 trillion in 2000 to US$19.50 trillion in 2025 in current dollars, and from 6th in the world to 2nd.

findings.title: Per person, a 936-fold gap
findings.body: GDP per person ranged from US$218,978 in Liechtenstein to US$234 in Burundi, a gap of 936 times.

climbers.name: Ghana
climbers.reason: Dollar GDP rose 37.1% against real growth of +6.0% and inflation of 14.2%. Most of the climb came from exchange-rate and price effects, not output.

climbers.name: Haiti
climbers.reason: Dollar GDP rose 32.2% against real growth of -2.7% and inflation of 28.6%. Real output shrank, so the climb came entirely from exchange-rate and price effects.

climbers.name: Zimbabwe
climbers.reason: Dollar GDP rose 23.3% against real growth of +8.1% and inflation of 81.4%. Real growth and exchange-rate and price effects both contributed.

climbers.name: Kyrgyzstan
climbers.reason: Dollar GDP rose 24.6% against real growth of +11.1% and inflation of 8.2%. Real growth and exchange-rate and price effects both contributed.

climbers.name: Tajikistan
climbers.reason: Dollar GDP rose 22.4% against real growth of +8.4% and inflation of 3.4%. Real growth and exchange-rate and price effects both contributed.

fallers.name: Venezuela
fallers.reason: Dollar GDP fell 17.3% against real growth of +1.6% and inflation of 252.0%. A weaker dollar value offset real growth and drove the fall.

fallers.name: Iran
fallers.reason: Dollar GDP fell 23.7% against real growth of -2.8% and inflation of 42.2%. Both output and the dollar value declined.

fallers.name: Ethiopia
fallers.reason: Dollar GDP fell 15.6% against real growth of +9.8% and inflation of 13.2%. A weaker dollar value offset real growth and drove the fall.

fallers.name: Trinidad and Tobago
fallers.reason: Dollar GDP rose 1.2% against real growth of -0.8% and inflation of 1.0%. Others grew faster in dollar terms and moved past it.

fallers.name: Libya
fallers.reason: Dollar GDP fell 0.8% against real growth of +13.4% and inflation of 1.8%. A weaker dollar value offset real growth and drove the fall.
